Real Estate

## AI AGENTS FOR REAL ESTATE.
 Brokerages and property managers win on speed. We build agents that answer every lead, book every showing, and keep every deal moving to close, around the clock.

 Book a Free Consultation
 How We Start

In Short
AI agents for real estate answer every lead within minutes, qualify buyers and renters, book showings on your calendar, and keep deals moving through the paperwork to close. Your agents and brokers stay in charge of pricing, negotiation, and relationships. We build around your CRM and your rules, and we start with one workflow.

 What We Build

### The Work That Piles Up.
 Real estate runs on response time and follow-through. Most of the lost deals trace back to a call nobody returned or a step nobody tracked.

#### Instant lead responseEvery web form, listing inquiry, and missed call gets a reply in seconds, with the details the prospect asked about.

#### Lead qualificationThe agent asks about timeline, budget, and area, then hands your team a qualified lead with the answers attached.

#### Showing schedulingIt checks calendars, offers times, confirms, reminds, and follows up afterward.

#### Transaction coordinationPaperwork checklists, document requests, and deadline reminders so every deal keeps moving to close.

#### Maintenance triageFor property managers: requests are sorted by urgency, tenants get updates, and vendors get routed work.

#### Past-client follow-upAnniversaries, market updates, and check-ins go out on schedule and feed your referral pipeline.

 Example

### A Tuesday at 9:47 p.m.

- A prospect submits a form on one of your listings.
- The agent replies within a minute with the listing details and asks about timeline and budget.
- It checks your agent's calendar and offers three showing times. The prospect picks one.
- It logs everything in your CRM and sends your agent a short summary.
- At 8 a.m. your agent opens a qualified lead with a showing already booked.

 Control

### Your People Stay In Charge.

- Negotiation and pricing. Agents handle speed and logistics. Your team handles offers, pricing advice, and the conversations that close.
- Scripts you approve. Agents follow the language and rules you set, and they escalate anything unusual to a person.
- A full record. Every message and action is logged, so you can see exactly what went out and when.
- Scoped access. Each agent connects only to the systems it needs.

 Questions

### Common Questions.

#### Which tools do you connect to?CRMs like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive, plus email, calendars, messaging, and the property or transaction platform you already use. We confirm the connections on the first call.

#### Will this replace my agents?No. It takes the response, scheduling, and paperwork work so your agents spend their time with clients.

#### Does it work after hours?Yes. That's the point. Leads get an answer at 9 p.m. the same as 9 a.m.

#### How long does a first build take?Most first builds go live in a few weeks. We scope the work up front so you know what you're getting.

 Finance runs on intake, matching, and approvals. We build agents that handle the volume so your team can focus on exceptions, analysis, and decisions.

 Book a Free Consultation
 How We Start

In Short
AI agents for finance handle invoice and PO intake, matching, approval routing, and the audit trail, so your team works the exceptions and approves the payments. Controls stay where they belong: scoped access, approval gates, and a full log. We start with the workflow that costs you the most hours.

 What We Build

### Where Back-Office Time Goes.
 Most finance teams don't struggle with hard decisions. They struggle with volume: keying data, finding the matching document, and chasing approvals.

#### Invoice and PO intakeAgents read invoices as they arrive, extract the fields, check the vendor, and create the record.

#### Three-way matchingInvoices are compared to POs and receipts. Clean matches post. Mismatches queue with a plain note.

#### Approval routingEach item goes to the right approver by your rules, with reminders and escalation when it stalls.

#### ReconciliationTransactions are matched across bank and ledger data, with exceptions explained and ready for review.

#### Audit preparationDocuments, approvals, and notes are assembled as the work happens, so audit requests are quick.

#### Reporting packetsRecurring reports are drafted from your data on schedule for an analyst to review and send.

 Example

### Invoice day, handled.

- Invoices arrive in the shared inbox in six different formats.
- The agent extracts vendor, amounts, dates, and line items, and checks the vendor against your approved list.
- It finds the matching PO and compares quantities and prices. One invoice is $420 over.
- Clean invoices route for approval. The $420 exception goes to a buyer with a one-line explanation.
- Every step lands in an audit log: who, what, when, and why.

 Control

### Controls Stay Where They Belong.

- Payment release. Your people approve payments above the limits you set. Agents prepare and route the work.
- Segregation of duties. Agents follow the same separation your policies require.
- Audit trail. Every action is logged in a form your auditors can read.
- Least-privilege access. Each agent sees only the systems and data its job needs.

#### How realistic are the benchmark numbers?They come from published studies, such as Ardent Partners' 2026 benchmark of $9.90 average and $2.67 best-in-class cost per invoice. Your results depend on volume, systems, and data quality, and we scope against your real numbers.

#### Will agents replace my accountants?No. They take the keying and matching so your team can spend time on exceptions, analysis, and advising.

 What We Build

### Admin That Never Bills.
 Attorneys lose a large share of their time to work that never shows up on an invoice. That's the layer agents are good at.

#### Client intakeAgents answer inquiries at any hour, ask your intake questions, and collect the documents a matter needs.

#### Document assemblyEngagement letters, forms, and routine documents are drafted from your templates for attorney review.

#### First-pass document reviewAgents flag clauses, missing items, and differences against your standards so attorneys start with a map.

#### Deadline trackingDates and tasks are tracked and reminders go out on schedule, so nothing depends on memory.

#### Time entry and billingDraft time entries and clear billing narratives come from calendars and documents, ready to confirm.

#### Client updatesStatus updates are drafted from the matter file for the responsible attorney to review and send.

 Example

### A new inquiry at 7:15 p.m.

- A prospective client submits an inquiry after the office closes.
- The agent asks your standard intake questions and collects the documents they have.
- It prepares the party information for your conflict-check process and flags the matter for staff.
- It drafts the engagement letter from your template and queues it for attorney approval.
- It offers consultation times from the attorney's calendar. The prospect books one.

 Control

### Attorneys Make The Calls.

- Judgment stays human. Agents prepare and organize. Attorneys review everything that carries legal judgment before it reaches a client.
- No legal advice from agents. Agents handle intake, drafting support, and admin. They don't advise clients.
- Confidentiality by design. We scope each agent's access to the matters and systems it needs and log every action.
- An audit trail. You can see what was drafted, what was sent, and who approved it.

 Example

# A Free AI Use Policy Template for Law Firms
By Derek Moore

Short answerA law firm AI use policy needs ten sections: scope, approved tools, data rules, attorney review, AI agents, client consent, billing, logging, incidents, and training. Below is a template you can copy or download as a Word file, built around the duties in ABA Formal Opinion 512.

 A template, and not legal advice. Adapt it with your ethics counsel, your state's rules, and any court-specific orders. Brackets mark where your firm fills in its own details.

 Download the Word template

### What Does a Law Firm AI Use Policy Need to Cover?

 A good policy answers the questions a partner, an associate, or a state bar investigator would ask: which tools, what data, who checks the output, what clients are told, how time is billed, and what gets logged. Each section ties back to a duty in Opinion 512.

 Policy section | Duty it supports | Model Rule | 

 Approved tools, data rules | Competence and confidentiality | 1.1, 1.6 | 

 Attorney review | Competence and candor to the tribunal | 1.1, 3.1, 3.3 | 

 AI agents, logging, incidents, training | Supervision | 5.1, 5.3 | 

 Client communication and consent | Communication | 1.4 | 

 Billing | Reasonable fees | 1.5 | 

 For the duty-by-duty reasoning, read our Opinion 512 checklist for AI agents.

### Why Does a Firm Need a Written Policy at All?

 Opinion 512 expects managerial lawyers to set clear policies on permissible uses of generative AI and to supervise how staff use it. A written policy turns that expectation into something you can train on and audit.

 The cost of skipping verification is public. In Mata v. Avianca, two New York lawyers filed a brief citing cases that ChatGPT had invented, and on June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel imposed a $5,000 penalty on the lawyers and their firm.

### The Template

 Copy it into your firm's format, or download the Word version.

#### [Firm Name] Generative AI Use Policy
Effective date: [date]  |  Owner: [Role]  |  Review: every 12 months and when tools or rules change

#### 1. Purpose and scope
This policy sets the rules for using generative AI at [Firm Name], including chatbots, drafting assistants, and AI agents. It applies to every attorney, paralegal, staff member, contractor, and vendor who works on firm matters.

It supports our duties under the Rules of Professional Conduct, including competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, candor to the tribunal, and reasonable fees.

#### 2. Approved tools
Only tools on the Approved Tools List may be used with firm or client information. [Role, e.g., the General Counsel or Managing Partner] keeps the list.

A tool is added only after review of its terms, data handling, security, and retention. Personal accounts and unapproved tools may not be used for firm work. To request a tool, [process].

#### 3. Data rules
Level 1, never entered into any AI tool: [e.g., sealed or court-protected material, government ID numbers, bank account numbers, health records].

Level 2, entered only into approved tools configured so our data is not used to train models: client confidential information and attorney work product.

Level 3, allowed in any approved tool: public information and firm marketing material.

#### 4. Attorney review and verification
A lawyer is responsible for everything produced with AI help. Before using AI output, the responsible lawyer must verify every citation, quotation, and factual claim against a primary source, and review the draft for accuracy, completeness, and tone.

AI output may not be filed with a court or sent to a client without attorney review. A person signs every filing.

#### 5. AI agents
An AI agent that takes actions, such as sending messages, updating records, or moving files, needs: a named owner; a written list of what it may access and do; least-privilege access; human approval before it sends anything to a client, files anything, or changes billing; a log of every action; and a way to switch it off immediately.

#### 6. Client communication and consent
Our engagement letter describes how we use AI in client matters. We obtain informed consent where the Rules or the client's instructions require it. Attorneys answer client questions about AI use honestly.

[Role] reviews the engagement-letter language every [12 months].

#### 7. Billing
We bill for time actually spent, including time spent reviewing AI output. We do not bill clients for time spent learning an AI tool. [Describe any flat-fee or per-task arrangements.]

#### 8. Logging and records
We record which tools were used on which matters, who used them, and who reviewed the output. Agent logs are kept for [period] and retained under our records policy.

#### 9. Incidents
Report any suspected leak of client information, any AI error that reached a client or a court, and any tool misuse to [Role] within [24 hours].

[Role] decides, with ethics counsel, whether to notify the client, the court, or our insurance carrier.

#### 10. Training, ownership, and review
Everyone completes AI training when they join and every [12 months]. [Role] owns this policy and reviews it at least once a year, and whenever tools, court rules, or ethics guidance change.

Violations are handled under [firm discipline policy].

#### AcknowledgmentI have read and will follow this policy. Name: ____________   Date: ____________

### How Do You Roll the Policy Out?

- Name an owner. One person is accountable for the policy and the tool list.

- Inventory what's already in use. Ask everyone, with amnesty, which AI tools they've tried. Shadow use is common.

- Approve a short list. Review terms and data handling, then publish the list.

- Train and acknowledge. A 30-minute session and a signed acknowledgment.

- Spot-check quarterly. Sample a few matters, confirm the log exists, and confirm review happened.

### How Do AI Agents Change the Policy?

 A chatbot answers questions. An agent acts: it sends messages, updates records, and moves files. Section 5 of the template covers the extra controls an agent needs, namely a named owner, scoped access, approval gates, a log, and an off switch.

 These are the controls we build into every AI agent for law firms. Our AI agent security guide goes deeper on access, data leakage, and audit trails.

### Frequently Asked Questions

#### Does a law firm need a written AI policy?

 ABA Formal Opinion 512 expects managerial lawyers to set clear firm policies on permissible uses of generative AI and to supervise how staff use it. Whether your state requires the policy in writing depends on its rules, so check with your state bar. A written policy is the simplest way to show you did it.

#### Can a lawyer bill a client for time spent using AI?

 Yes, for the time actually spent. The ABA gives this example: if a lawyer spends 15 minutes entering information into a tool to draft a pleading, the lawyer may bill that time and the time spent reviewing the draft. In most circumstances a lawyer can't bill a client for the time it takes to learn how to use the tool.

#### Do we have to tell clients we use AI?

 Rule 1.4 requires reasonable consultation with the client about the means used to reach their objectives, and Rule 1.6 protects client information unless the client gives informed consent. Many firms address AI in the engagement letter. Your state's guidance may say more, so check it.

#### What happened in Mata v. Avianca?

 Two New York lawyers filed a brief that cited cases ChatGPT had invented. On June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel of the Southern District of New York imposed a $5,000 penalty on the lawyers and their firm, and the case is a widely cited example of why attorney verification belongs in every AI policy.

 New York firms: see our page on AI agents for New York firms, which links the NYSBA and NYC Bar resources.

### Sources

- American Bar Association, ABA issues first ethics guidance on a lawyer's use of AI tools (July 29, 2024)
- American Bar Association, Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools (July 29, 2024)
- Mata v. Avianca, Inc., Opinion and Order on sanctions, No. 1:22-cv-01461 (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023)
- Muchman, Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools: ABA Formal Opinion 512 Provides Needed Guidance, The Bar Examiner (Fall 2024)
- New York State Bar Association, Report and Recommendations of the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024)

 The template is a starting point. State rules and court orders can differ, so check yours.

# AP Automation for Small Accounting Firms: Software or Custom Agent?
By Derek Moore

Short answerBuy AP software when your invoices, approvals, and accounting system fit its standard workflow, and build a custom agent when your rules, clients, or systems don't. Many small firms do both: software for the common path, an agent for the exceptions. Pilot on three months of old invoices before you trust either.

 This applies to a firm's own payables and to the AP work an accounting or bookkeeping practice runs for clients. The same decision comes up in both.

### What Does AP Cost Per Invoice, and Where Does the Time Go?

 Ardent Partners' 2026 benchmark puts the average cost to process one invoice at $9.90. Best-in-Class teams (the 20% with the lowest cost and shortest cycle times) process one for $2.67. Nearly 1 in 5 invoices hits an exception, and Best-in-Class teams hold that to 11.8%.

 $9.90

 average cost to process one invoice (Ardent Partners, 2026)

 $2.67

 cost for Best-in-Class teams

 72%

 of finance organizations spend up to 520 hours a year on manual AP (CFO Research, 2020)

 Here is what that gap means at small-firm volume, as an illustration. At 300 invoices a month, $9.90 each is $35,640 a year and $2.67 each is $9,612. The difference is about $26,000 a year.

 Those benchmarks come from larger-company surveys, so your numbers will differ. Our ROI calculator lets you run your own volume and hourly cost.

### What Does AP Software Do Well?

 AP software is the category with products like Bill, Ramp, Dext, and Stampli. We name them for orientation only, with no ranking or endorsement.

 The category handles the common path well:

- Capturing invoices from email and reading the fields

- Coding to your chart of accounts

- Routing approvals by amount or department

- Paying vendors and syncing to your accounting system

 It's fast to start, the vendor maintains it, and the upfront cost is low. For a firm with one entity and a standard approval chain, it's often the right answer.

### Where Does AP Software Run Out of Road?

 Software is built for the standard workflow, so friction starts where your work isn't standard:

- Many clients, different rules. Each client has its own coding rules, approvers, and thresholds, and each one needs its own setup.

- Messy inputs. Scans, photos, and one-off formats still land in an exception queue.

- Matching beyond the basics. Checking an invoice against a PO, a receipt, and a contract term takes logic the product may not offer.

- Unusual systems. If your ledger or approval tool has no clean integration, people re-key data by hand.

- Exceptions. Software flags the problem. A person still researches it, drafts the fix, and chases the answer.

### What Does a Custom AP Agent Do?

 An agent does the work around the invoice as well as the keying. A typical build reads each invoice and checks the vendor against your master list. It matches the PO, codes the invoice using each client's rules, and routes it for approval.

 On an exception, it works out what's wrong. It might be an invoice $420 over its PO or a new bank account on a known vendor. The agent sends a person a one-line note with the evidence attached, and logs every step for the auditor.

 An agent can also work inside the software you already run, the way an employee would. We cover that in agents that use your software.

### Software or Custom Agent: How Do You Decide?

 | AP software | Custom AP agent | 

 Time to start | Fastest | Slower: needs build and testing | 

 Fit to your rules | Configure within the product's options | Built around your rules | 

 Many clients, different rules | Usually one setup per client | One agent applying each client's rules | 

 Odd formats and exceptions | Flags them for a person to fix | Researches, drafts the fix, routes a clean exception | 

 Upfront cost | Lower | Higher | 

 Ongoing cost | Per-user or per-volume fees | Hosting, model usage, and support | 

 Who maintains it | The vendor | You or your build partner | 

 Best when | Standard workflow, one entity | Custom rules, many clients, messy inputs | 

 Choose software if your approval chain is simple, your invoices are mostly clean, and your accounting system has a supported integration.

 Choose a custom agent if you run AP for many clients with different rules, your exception queue eats real hours, or your systems don't connect cleanly.

 Choose both if software handles the clean 80% and an agent works the exceptions and the cross-system matching. This is the setup we'd test first for most small firms.

### What Controls Should Any AP Automation Have?

 Whichever route you pick, these controls stay the same:

- Separation of duties. The automation never approves and releases the same payment on its own.

- Approval thresholds. Anything above a set amount goes to a person.

- Vendor change checks. A new bank account on a known vendor triggers a call-back to a number you already have on file. The FBI's 2024 Internet Crime Report lists business email compromise at $2.77 billion in reported losses.

- Duplicate detection. Same vendor, same amount, same week gets flagged.

- A complete log. Every read, match, and routing decision is recorded and reviewable.

- Least-privilege access. The automation sees only the ledgers and clients it needs.

### How Do You Test Before You Trust It?

- Shadow mode. Run the tool on the last three months of invoices without paying anything. Compare its coding, matching, and flags to what your team actually did.

- Measure. Track match accuracy, exception rate, and time per invoice against your own baseline and the benchmarks above.

- Supervised live. Let it work real invoices with a person approving every one for a few weeks.

- Widen slowly. Raise the auto-route limits only for categories that stay clean.

 For the wider back-office picture, see AI for finance teams and AI for accounting, or the work we do in AI agents for finance.

### Sources

- Ardent Partners, Accounts Payable Metrics that Matter in 2026 (summary of findings: average $9.90 and Best-in-Class $2.67 per invoice; exception rates)
- Ardent Partners, AP Metrics that Matter in 2026, report page (average cost and cycle time)
- CFO Research, survey of finance organizations on manual accounts payable work (Business Wire, July 28, 2020)
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2024 Internet Crime Report (business email compromise losses of $2,770,151,146)

 Benchmarks come from larger-company surveys. Run your own volume and costs before you decide.

#### Not Sure Whether Software or an Agent Fits?
 We'll look at your invoice volume, your clients' rules, and your systems, and tell you honestly which route makes sense, including when software alone is enough. Book a free 30-minute consultation.

# Speed to Lead for Real Estate: The AI Response Playbook
By Derek Moore

Short answerReply within 5 minutes, at any hour, with a message that asks one question and offers a showing time. The best-known study found the odds of reaching a lead fall 100 times between a 5-minute and a 30-minute response. Below are the numbers, the scripts, and the point where a person takes over.

### How Fast Should a Real Estate Lead Get a Response?

 Inside 5 minutes. The most-cited research is the InsideSales.com and MIT Lead Response Management Study, which tracked six companies, more than 15,000 leads, and over 100,000 call attempts across three years.

 It found that the odds of contacting a lead drop 100 times when the first call comes at 30 minutes instead of 5. The odds of qualifying that lead drop 21 times.

 100x

 drop in the odds of reaching a lead, 5 minutes vs. 30 (MIT and InsideSales.com, 2007)

 8x

 higher conversion rate in the first five minutes (InsideSales, 2021)

 0.1%

 of inbound leads were engaged in under 5 minutes (InsideSales, 2021)

 A 2021 InsideSales analysis of 5.7 million inbound leads at more than 400 companies found the same pattern. Conversion rates were 8 times greater in the first five minutes, and only 0.1% of leads got a response that fast.

 Harvard Business Review's 2011 study of online leads found the average company took 42 hours to respond, and nearly a quarter never responded at all.

 How to read these numbers. The studies cover many industries and were run or funded by a lead-response vendor, and the 2007 data is about phone calls. Treat the exact multiples as direction, because the direction has held for years and your own CRM will show how it plays out in your market.

### Why Do Leads Go Cold So Fast?

 A lead who fills out a form at 9:47 p.m. is on their phone, interested, and looking at other listings. That moment of attention doesn't last.

 The first reply that sounds like a person and offers a time usually gets the conversation. A reply the next morning arrives after the prospect has already talked to someone else.

 Agents can't be available every hour. They're at showings, in closings, and asleep. That gap is the job for an AI response agent.

### What Does an AI Response Agent Do in the First Five Minutes?

- Seconds 0 to 10. A form, portal inquiry, or missed call arrives. The agent logs the lead in your CRM and tags the source and listing.

- Seconds 10 to 60. It sends a text and an email that name the listing, say who it is, and ask one question.

- Minutes 1 to 3. It answers simple questions from your listing data (price, availability, HOA, open house times) and asks about timeline and budget.

- By minute 5. It offers two or three showing times pulled from the agent's real calendar, and books the one the lead picks.

- Anything else. It stops and hands the conversation to a person, with a short summary of what the lead said.

 The agent works your lead sources, your CRM, and your calendar. It isn't a separate inbox to check.

### What Should the First Message Say? Four Scripts

 Every first message does four things: names the listing, says who is writing, asks one question, and gives an easy way to opt out of texts. Use these as starting points and put them in your own voice.

 1. New web lead, daytimeHi [Name], it's [Agent] at [Brokerage]. Thanks for asking about [Address]. Are you hoping to see it this week? I have [Day] at [time] or [Day] at [time]. Reply STOP to opt out.

 2. New lead after hoursHi [Name], thanks for reaching out about [Address] tonight. I'm the AI assistant for [Agent] at [Brokerage], and I can help right now. Are you looking to buy or rent, and when would you like to move? Reply STOP to opt out.

 3. Open house follow-up, same dayHi [Name], thanks for coming to [Address] today. What did you think of it? If you'd like a second look, or want to see similar homes, I can set up a time. Reply STOP to opt out.

 4. Missed call text-backSorry we missed your call to [Brokerage]. I'm the AI assistant for [Agent]. What can I help with? I can answer questions about [Address] or book a showing. Reply STOP to opt out.

 Tell people when they're talking to an assistant. It builds trust, and most leads care more about the fast, useful answer than who typed it.

### Where Does a Person Take Over?

 The agent handles speed, scheduling, and simple answers. A licensed agent handles judgment. Set these handoffs in writing before launch:

- Pricing advice, offers, negotiation, and anything that sounds like a commitment

- Questions about who lives in a neighborhood, or any request that touches a protected class (the agent must never steer or comment, and passes these to a person)

- Any lead who asks for a human, sounds upset, or has a complicated situation

- Any question the agent can't answer from your listing data

 The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing, and the agent's rules need to reflect that. Your broker or counsel should review the script set before it goes live.

### What About Texting Consent?

 Texting prospects is covered by the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. Collect clear consent on the form that creates the lead, honor opt-outs right away, and keep a record of the consent.

 The rules around texting change, so have your counsel confirm the language on your forms.

### How Do You Measure It?

 Start with a baseline from your CRM for the last 30 days, then track the same five numbers every week:

- Median time to first reply

- Share of leads answered in under 5 minutes

- Contact rate (leads who replied or picked up)

- Showings booked per 100 leads

- Leads that become clients

 One free test you can run today: submit a lead through your own website at 9:47 p.m. on a Friday and time the reply. If you can't beat 5 minutes, you've found the first thing to fix.

 To put dollars on the gap, run your numbers through our free ROI calculator.

### What Does Setup Involve?

 Most of the work is connecting your lead sources, your CRM, and the agent's calendar, then writing the rules for what the agent may say and when it hands off. We build this as part of our AI agents for real estate work, with approval gates on anything a client sees that carries judgment.

### Sources

- InsideSales.com and MIT (Oldroyd), How Much Time Do You Have Before Web-Generated Leads Go Cold?, the Lead Response Management Study (2007; six companies, three years of data, 15,000+ leads, 100,000+ call attempts)
- InsideSales, Lead Response Study 2021 (5.7 million inbound leads, 400+ companies)
- Oldroyd, McElheran, and Elkington, The Short Life of Online Sales Leads, Harvard Business Review (March 2011)
- U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Fair Housing Act overview
- Federal Communications Commission, Stop Unwanted Robocalls and Texts

 Response-time studies cover many industries. Check texting and fair housing rules with your broker or counsel.

#### Want Every Lead Answered in Minutes?
 We build lead-response agents for brokerages and property teams, wired into your CRM and calendar. Book a free 30-minute consultation and we'll map where your leads wait today.

URL: https://aismartr.com/blog-aba-opinion-512-ai-agents-law-firms.html
# ABA Formal Opinion 512, Translated Into Controls for AI Agents
By Derek Moore

Short answerABA Formal Opinion 512 applies the existing Rules of Professional Conduct to generative AI. For an AI agent, that means testing it before live matters, limiting its access to client data, deciding when to tell clients, supervising its output, verifying anything filed, and billing only real time. A seven-point policy starter is below.

 A practical guide, and not legal advice. Your ethics counsel and your state's rules have the final word. We build the agents. You decide what's permitted.

### What Does ABA Formal Opinion 512 Say?

 On July 29, 2024, the ABA's Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility issued Formal Opinion 512, "Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools." It's the ABA's first formal opinion on lawyers' use of generative AI.

 The core message is simple. The rules you already follow still apply. The opinion works through six areas: competence, confidentiality, communication with clients, supervision, candor to the tribunal, and fees.

 An AI agent doesn't change those duties. It changes where you have to apply them.

### What Should a Firm Do With an AI Agent, Duty by Duty?

#### Competence (Model Rule 1.1)

 Lawyers need a reasonable understanding of the benefits and risks of the technology they use. The opinion also warns that relying on a tool's output without appropriate independent verification can fall short of the competence duty.

- Test every agent on real, past matters before it touches a live one.

- Require attorney review for anything that carries legal judgment.

- Keep a log of what the agent produced and who approved it.

#### Confidentiality (Model Rule 1.6)

 Client information has to stay protected, including when it's entered into an AI tool. The opinion points lawyers to the risk that information is disclosed or accessed by others, and to reviewing a tool's terms and privacy practices.

- Give each agent access only to the matters and systems it needs.

- Review the terms and data handling of every tool and model the agent uses.

- Decide in writing what client data may enter an agent, and what may not.

#### Communication (Model Rule 1.4)

 Lawyers have to keep clients reasonably informed, which includes thinking about when AI use should be disclosed.

- Decide when your firm tells clients about AI use, and put that language in your engagement letter.

- Answer client questions about how agents are used with a consistent, honest script.

#### Supervision (Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3)

 Managerial lawyers are expected to set clear firm policies on permissible uses of generative AI and to supervise how staff use it.

- Write an AI use policy and train everyone on it.

- Treat agent output the way you'd treat a junior colleague's work: reviewed before it goes out.

#### Candor to the tribunal (Model Rules 3.1 and 3.3)

 Anything filed with a court has to be accurate and verified, whatever drafted it.

- Verify every citation and quotation independently.

- Keep agents out of the final filing step. A person signs.

#### Fees (Model Rule 1.5)

 Fees must stay reasonable. The ABA's example: if a lawyer spends 15 minutes entering information into a tool to draft a pleading, the lawyer may bill that time and the time spent reviewing the draft. In most circumstances a lawyer can't bill a client for the time it takes to learn how to use the tool.

- Bill the time you actually spend, including review.

- Don't bill clients for learning a tool.

### What Should New York Lawyers Know?

 New York lawyers have more to read. The New York State Bar Association's Task Force on Artificial Intelligence published its report and recommendations in April 2024, covering the legal, social, and ethical impact of AI on the profession. The Association of the City of New York Bar published a May 2025 compilation of current ethics opinions and reports on generative AI across jurisdictions.

 Check your own state's rules and any court-specific orders before you deploy anything.

### What Goes in a Seven-Point AI Policy?

- Approved tools. A short list of tools and models the firm has reviewed.

- Data rules. What client information may enter an agent, and what may not.

- Review rule. Which outputs need attorney approval before they're used.

- Client disclosure. When and how you tell clients.

- Billing rule. How AI-assisted work is recorded and billed.

- Logging. A record of what each agent did, and who approved it.

- Training and review. Onboarding for new staff and an annual refresh as the tools change.

 Want the full text? Get our free AI use policy template for law firms, with all ten sections and a Word download.

#### How We Build Agents For Firms That Follow These Rules

- Scoped, least-privilege access to the matters and systems an agent needs

- Approval gates on anything that carries legal judgment or goes to a client

- A full log of every action, in a form you can review

- No legal advice from agents. Attorneys make the calls.

### Sources

- American Bar Association, ABA issues first ethics guidance on a lawyer's use of AI tools (July 29, 2024)
- American Bar Association, Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools (July 29, 2024)
- Muchman, Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools: ABA Formal Opinion 512 Provides Needed Guidance, The Bar Examiner (Fall 2024)
- New York State Bar Association, Report and Recommendations of the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024)
- Association of the Bar of the City of New York, Current Ethics Opinions and Reports Related to Generative Artificial Intelligence (May 2025)

 Opinion 512 is the ABA's guidance. State rules and court orders can differ, so check yours.

# Your Firm Loses Clients Before They're Clients. Fix Intake and Onboarding With AI.
By Derek Moore

Short answerAn AI intake agent replies to every inquiry the moment it arrives, identifies the matter or service type, explains the process, and offers times to book, while a person stays in charge of anything that needs judgment. Clio's test of 500 law firms shows how often firms fail that first contact.

 The short version: Intake and onboarding are high-volume, rules-based, and time-sensitive, which makes them a strong fit for agents. Let the agent respond, collect, check, and chase. Keep a person on conflicts, engagement terms, risk decisions, and the first real conversation.

 A prospective client fills in your contact form at 6:40 on a Tuesday evening. What happens next decides more revenue than most firms realize. At a lot of firms the answer is "nothing until someone gets to it."

 Clio tested this directly. For its 2024 Legal Trends Report, it hired a third-party research company to contact 500 law firms by email and phone with a client inquiry. The results were not close to good.

 48%

 of law firms were unreachable by phone, even after a chance to return messages (Clio)

 33%

 of law firms responded to an emailed client inquiry (Clio)

 70%

 of financial institutions lost clients in the past year to inefficient onboarding (Fenergo)

 The third number comes from the other end of the funnel. Fenergo's 2025 Financial Crime Industry Trends Report surveyed 600 senior decision-makers at banks, asset managers, and fund administrators. Seventy percent said their firm lost clients in the past year because onboarding was slow or inefficient, up from 48% two years earlier. Abandonment during onboarding averaged around 10%.

 Those are two different industries and two different stages, and neither study covers every kind of firm. They point at the same leak, though: people who already decided to hire you, or were close to it, and left because the front door was slow.

### Why Do Intake and Onboarding Break?

 Nobody designs a bad intake process on purpose. It breaks for structural reasons that are the same at a six-person law firm, a wealth advisory practice, a brokerage, and an accounting firm.

- It belongs to nobody. Intake sits between marketing, the front desk, and the professionals who do the billable work. Each assumes another one has it.

- It competes with billable hours. A reply to a stranger always loses to a deadline for a paying client.

- It arrives outside office hours. People look for a lawyer, an advisor, or an agent when their own workday ends.

- It is repetitive but not identical. Every matter needs the same ten things, but which ten depends on the matter type, the entity, and the jurisdiction. That is too variable for a static form and too tedious for a senior person.

- The chasing never ends. The engagement letter is out for signature. The ID is blurry. The second owner hasn't sent their documents. Someone has to remember all of it.

 Clio's shoppers also reported that when they did reach a firm, 73% were unlikely to recommend it. Being reachable is the minimum. Being useful on first contact is the actual bar.

### What Does an AI Agent Do in Intake and Onboarding?

 An intake and onboarding agent is not a chatbot bolted onto the website. It is a worker with access to your inbox, calendar, CRM or practice management system, document storage, and e-signature tool, running a defined process. Here is the work it can own.

#### 1. First response in minutes, at any hour
 The agent reads the inquiry, identifies the matter or service type, and replies with something specific: what the process looks like, what the consultation covers, and available times to book. Clio found that only 36% of firms reached by phone could explain the process and next steps. An agent can do that on every inquiry because it is reading from your own playbook.

#### 2. Qualification against your criteria
 You decide what a good-fit client looks like: practice area, geography, matter size, account minimum, timeline. The agent asks the questions needed to place the inquiry, records the answers, and routes it. Good fits get a booking link. Poor fits get a polite decline and, if you want, a referral.

#### 3. Document and information collection
 Instead of one long form, the agent requests what this specific client needs, checks what comes back, and asks again for anything missing or unreadable. It extracts names, dates, entity details, and account information into structured fields so nobody retypes them.

#### 4. Preparing the checks that a person approves
 The agent can run a new client's name and related parties against your client list and flag possible conflicts. It can assemble a KYC or due-diligence packet and note what is missing. It does not clear the conflict or accept the risk. It hands a reviewer a prepared file with the open questions at the top.

#### 5. Engagement paperwork and system setup
 Once a person approves, the agent generates the engagement letter from your template, sends it for signature, follows up until it is signed, then opens the matter or account, creates the folder structure, sets up billing, and schedules the kickoff.

#### 6. Status updates nobody has to write
 Clients get told where they are in the process and what is still needed. Your team gets a single view of every onboarding in flight and what each one is waiting on.

### Where Does a Person Stay in Charge?

 This is a regulated, trust-based workflow. Getting the division of labor wrong creates real exposure, so draw the line on purpose.

#### Keep These Decisions Human

- Conflict clearance. The agent surfaces possible conflicts. A responsible professional decides.

- Accepting or declining a client where judgment is involved, including anything touching risk rating or source of funds.

- Fees and engagement terms that depart from your standard template.

- Anything that could be read as advice. The agent explains your process. It does not assess someone's legal position, tax situation, or investments.

- The first substantive conversation. Speed gets the meeting. A person wins the relationship.

 Two more rules belong in the build from day one. Tell people when they are dealing with an AI assistant, and give them a way to reach a person at every step. And check your own obligations before go-live: professional conduct rules on confidentiality and supervision for law firms, books-and-records and KYC requirements for financial firms, and whatever your regulator or insurer says about automated client communication. Those rules vary by profession and state, so confirm them with whoever owns compliance at your firm.

### What Does the Agent Need Access To?

 Most of the effort in this project is integration, not AI. The agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach.

- Inbound channels: web forms, the shared inbox, and ideally missed-call and voicemail transcripts

- Calendar: real availability, so it books meetings instead of proposing them

- System of record: practice management, CRM, or portfolio system, with write access limited to the fields it needs

- Documents and e-signature: your templates, a secure upload link, and signature status

- Your playbook: qualification criteria, required documents by matter type, and escalation rules, written down

 Client intake data is some of the most sensitive information you hold. Scope access tightly, log every action the agent takes, keep client documents inside systems you already trust, and confirm how any AI vendor in the chain handles and retains data.

### How Do You Roll It Out in 30 Days Without Betting the Firm?

#### Week 1: Map and measure
 Write down the current process for one matter or client type, step by step. Pull the last quarter of inquiries and record how long first response took, how many booked, how many signed, and how long signing to kickoff took. If you can't get those numbers, that is your first finding.

#### Week 2: First response and booking only
 Turn on the narrowest useful piece. The agent drafts replies and a person sends them for the first few days. When the drafts stop needing edits, let it send.

#### Week 3: Collection and chasing
 Add document requests, completeness checks, and reminders. This is usually where staff feel the difference, because the chasing is the part everyone hates.

#### Week 4: Prepared approvals and setup
 Add conflict and due-diligence preparation with a human approval step, then engagement letters and system setup after approval. Review every escalation from the month and adjust the rules.

### What Should You Measure?

 Skip vanity metrics. Four numbers tell you whether this is working, and you should compare each against the baseline you took in week one.

- Time to first response, measured in minutes, including nights and weekends

- Inquiry-to-consultation rate: of the people who contacted you, how many got on the calendar

- Days from yes to fully onboarded: signed, documents in, matter or account open

- Staff hours per new client spent on intake and setup

 Track one quality check alongside them: how often a person had to correct something the agent did. That number should fall over the first month. If it doesn't, the playbook is unclear, and no model will fix an unclear playbook.

### Where Should You Start?

 Run Clio's test on yourself. Have someone outside the firm submit an inquiry by web form at 7 pm and call the main line at lunch. Time the response and read it as a stranger would. If the result bothers you, you have found the highest-return automation project in the building, and it is one where the agent's work is easy to verify and the downside is contained by a human approval step.

# AI Automation for Finance Teams: Invoices, Purchase Orders, and Faster Approvals
By Derek Moore

Short answerAI agents take over invoice and PO intake, matching, and approval routing in back-office finance. An agent compares quantities, prices, and terms across documents, posts the clean matches, and queues mismatches with a plain-language note, so your team resolves exceptions and approves payments instead of keying data.

### Where Does Back-Office Time Actually Go?

 Most finance teams don't struggle with hard decisions. They struggle with volume: keying invoice data, hunting for the matching PO, chasing a manager for an approval, and rebuilding the trail when an auditor asks.

 That work is repetitive, rule-based, and spread across email, shared drives, and an ERP. It's the ideal shape for an AI agent.

$9.90

average cost to process one invoice (Ardent Partners, 2026)

cost for Best-in-Class teams

1 in 5

invoices hit an exception (Ardent Partners, 2026)

These are published benchmarks from larger-company surveys. Your results depend on your volume, your systems, and how clean your data is.

### How Does AI Handle Invoice and PO Intake?

 An intake agent watches the shared inbox and the upload folder. It reads each invoice, extracts the vendor, amounts, dates, and line items, and creates the record in your system.

 It checks the vendor against your approved list and flags anything unusual: a new bank account, a duplicate invoice number, or an amount that doesn't fit the PO. Clean invoices move forward on their own.

### How Does AI Handle Matching and Reconciliation?

 Matching an invoice to its PO and receipt is the step where small differences cause big delays.

 An agent compares quantities, prices, and terms across the documents, then posts the clean matches and queues the mismatches with a plain-language note: "Invoice is $420 over the PO. Receipt shows 40 units delivered, PO says 50." Your team resolves the exception instead of hunting for it.

### How Do Approvals and the Audit Trail Work?

 Approvals stall because people don't see them. An agent routes each item to the right approver based on your rules, sends reminders, and escalates when something sits too long.

 Every action lands in a log: who approved what, when, and on what basis. When the audit arrives, the trail already exists.

 Approval gates stay in place. Agents prepare and route the work. Your people approve payments above the limits you set.

### How Does AI Help With Vendor Follow-Up and Procurement?

 Procurement has its own repetitive loop: request quotes, compare them, chase missing documents, and confirm delivery dates. An agent can send the requests, collect the replies into a comparison, and follow up with vendors who haven't answered.

 Your buyer reviews a ready comparison and makes the call.

 Software or custom agent? Our guide to AP automation for small firms compares both, with 2026 cost benchmarks and the controls to keep.

### Where Should You Start?

 Start with invoice intake. It has the highest volume, the clearest rules, and the easiest measurement: invoices processed, time to post, and exceptions caught.

 Add matching and approval routing next. Packaged agents connected to your existing ERP typically go live in four to eight weeks.

# Human-in-the-Loop AI Agents: When Should a Person Step In?
By Derek Moore

Short answerKeep a human in the loop wherever trust carries the relationship. Adobe's 2026 report found customers are more comfortable when an agent works with a brand's human representative (45%) than when it makes a final decision alone (21%). Let agents run alone on routine work, and design the handoff to a person along with the agent.

 Decision | Agent runs alone | Person stays in the loop | 
Stakes | Low-stakes, reversible steps such as scheduling and status updates | Anything legal, financial, or hard to reverse | 
Money | Order and status lookups | Refunds, credits, and pricing exceptions above your threshold | 
Conversations | Routing and triage to the right team | Complaints and emotionally charged conversations | 
Output | Drafts and summaries for review, auditable record updates | Low-confidence cases, or when the customer asks for a person | 

 Trust is the product. Clients hand you their money, their legal problems, and their biggest purchase. Let agents handle speed and logistics, and keep a person on every moment that needs judgment or reassurance.

 Adobe's 2026 AI and Digital Trends Report looked at how organizations and consumers feel about AI agents doing real work. 78% of organizations expect agentic AI to handle about half or more of their customer support interactions within the next 18 months.

 The open question is how customers feel when it does. Those numbers tell a different story.

 45%

 of consumers comfortable with an AI agent working directly with a brand's human rep

 21%

 of consumers comfortable with an agent making a final decision on its own

 16%

 of organizations with agentic AI embedded org-wide for customer support

### What Is the Comfort Gap, and Why Is It a Design Brief?

 Customers are noticeably more comfortable when their personal AI agent works with a brand's human representative (45%) than when it makes a final decision without anyone stepping in (21%). Businesses are more permissive than their customers on every one of these measures: 55% versus 45% for agent-plus-human, and 35% versus 21% for autonomous final decisions. On large, complex purchases handled entirely by an agent, it's 29% of businesses versus 16% of consumers.

 Read that as a spec for agents: let the agent do the work and let a human own the consequential decision.

### Where Should an Agent Run Alone?

- Low-stakes, reversible steps such as scheduling, rescheduling, status updates, and order lookups

- Record updates and data entry that can be audited later

- Drafting replies and summaries for a person to review

- Routing and triage to the right team

### Where Should a Human Stay in the Loop?

- Refunds, credits, and pricing exceptions above a threshold you set

- Complaints and emotionally charged conversations

- Anything legal, financial, or hard to reverse

- Any case where the agent's confidence is low or the customer asks for a person

 Make the handoff a feature. "Let me bring in a teammate who has the full context" beats a dead end every time, as long as the agent actually passes the context along.

### How Do You Design the Handoff?

 The weak point in most customer-facing agents is the transition. A good handoff passes the full conversation, what the agent already tried, and what the customer needs, so the customer never repeats themselves.

 Set explicit escalation triggers: low confidence, negative sentiment, repeated rephrasing, or a direct request for a person. And tell customers when they're talking to AI. Trust is easier to keep than to rebuild.

### How Do You Get Found by Other Agents?

 The same Adobe report found that only 13% of organizations have embedded agentic AI organization-wide for brand discovery, meaning content optimized so AI-powered search can interpret and surface it. It also found that roughly half of organizations say an agent's ability to interact with other agents is a crucial factor when choosing vendors.

 As customers' own assistants start researching on their behalf, being clearly described, well structured, and easy to cite becomes part of being found. Clear service pages, structured data, an llms.txt file, and content that answers the exact questions customers ask are a practical place to start.

#### A Safe Rollout Pattern
 Start with one customer-facing workflow. Let the agent prepare and draft, and have a human approve. Track resolution time and customer satisfaction for a month. Where the numbers hold, widen the agent's authority one step at a time.

### Where Should You Start?

 Pick the customer interaction where your team loses the most time to repetition, and map which steps are reversible. Automate those first, put approvals on the rest, and let results decide how much autonomy the agent earns.

 Before an agent touches client data, read our guide to AI agent security risks and best practices.

### Sources

- Adobe, 2026 AI and Digital Trends Report (Oxford Economics survey of 3,000 executives and practitioners and 4,000 customers, fielded October to November 2025)

#### Want agents your customers actually trust?
 We design customer-facing agents with the right handoffs, approval gates, and escalation rules built in from day one.

 Source: Adobe 2026 AI and Digital Trends Report.

# Half of Companies Now Get Value From AI. What Separates the Top 7.5%?
By Derek Moore

Short answerAlmost half of companies now generate value from AI, according to BCG's 2026 Applied AI Index, and the most mature 7.5% generate roughly 2.4 times the top-line growth of laggards. Agents still miss about one in three real computer tasks on a Stanford benchmark, so keep people approving consequential steps.

 The leaders' playbook. Pick specific processes, measure them, and keep people in charge of the judgment calls. That works at any firm size.

 For two years the AI question was whether it works. BCG's 2026 Applied AI Index, published in September, suggests that question is settled: almost half of companies now generate value from AI, and 41% are in the scaling stage.

 The more interesting number is the gap. BCG reports that its most mature 7.5% of companies, which it calls "future-built," generate roughly 2.4 times the top-line growth of laggards, and they do it through enterprise-wide programs.

 ~50%

 of companies now generate value from AI (BCG, 2026)

 7.5%

 "future-built" leaders at about 2.4x the top-line growth of laggards

 ~66%

 agent task success on OSWorld, up from 12% (Stanford AI Index 2026)

### Is the AI Experiment Phase Over?

 The numbers reward AI tied to real workflows, with owners, targets, and measurement. If your AI work is still "a few people trying ChatGPT," you're in the group the leaders are pulling away from.

### What Do the AI Leaders Have in Common?

 BCG's finding is that the leaders run enterprise-wide programs. Translated to a smaller company, here's our read of what that looks like in practice:

- One named owner per automated workflow, accountable for the result

- A baseline measured before automating (hours, cost, error rate), so ROI is provable

- A few workflows done deeply instead of many tools adopted shallowly

- AI built into the systems people already use, with no separate tab to remember

- Review checkpoints wherever a mistake is expensive

 Leaders treat AI as an operating change with owners and metrics, and budget size matters less than that discipline.

### How Reliable Are AI Agents Today?

 Stanford's 2026 AI Index reports that AI agents jumped from roughly 12% to about 66% task success on OSWorld, a benchmark of real computer tasks across operating systems. That's a remarkable leap. It also means agents still fail roughly one in three attempts on structured benchmarks.

 Read it both ways. Agents are now capable enough to own real workflow steps, and not reliable enough to run unsupervised on anything expensive to get wrong. Approval gates, logging, and test sets matter more as agents improve.

### What Does the Gap Mean for a Firm Your Size?

 You don't need an enterprise program. You need the same discipline at a smaller scale: pick the two or three workflows where hours leak the most, name an owner, measure the baseline, automate with approval gates, and review the numbers every month.

#### A 90-Day Plan
 Days 1 to 30: List your workflows, measure hours and error rates, and pick the top three by time lost.

 Days 31 to 60: Automate the first one, with human approval on any consequential step.

 Days 61 to 90: Compare results to the baseline, tune, and start the second workflow.

### Where Should You Start?

 Start with the baseline. If you can't say how many hours a workflow costs you today, you can't prove what automating it saved, and that's the difference between AI that gets renewed in the budget and AI that quietly gets cut.

URL: https://aismartr.com/blog-model-agnostic-ai-automation.html
# Model Prices Just Dropped 80%. Is Your Automation Built to Use It?
By Derek Moore

Short answerModel-agnostic automation treats the AI model as a setting you can change, so a price cut or a better model means a quick swap and no rebuild. Teams hard-wired to one provider scramble when prices or rankings move. Match the model to the task, and keep a small test set for each workflow.

 Match the model to the task. A small, cheap model can sort invoices and intake forms. A stronger one can handle contract review and client-facing drafts.

 On July 30, OpenAI announced that GPT-5.6 Luna would cost 80% less and GPT-5.6 Terra 20% less. The new API pricing: $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens for Terra, and $0.20 and $1.20 for Luna.

 That's one provider on one day. This summer also brought GPT-5.6 in three tiers (Sol, Terra, and Luna), Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, and Meta's Muse Code for background coding agents. The leaderboard keeps changing, and so does the price list.

 So here's the question every business running AI automation should be able to answer: if a better or cheaper model shipped tomorrow, how long would it take you to switch?

 80%

 price cut to GPT-5.6 Luna on July 30

 20%

 price cut to GPT-5.6 Terra the same day

 3

 tiers in the GPT-5.6 family: Sol, Terra, Luna

### What Does Model Lock-In Actually Cost?

 When your prompts, tools, and workflow logic are written around one model's quirks, every change becomes a project. You can't capture a price cut.

 You can't move a hard task to a stronger model. And an outage or policy change at one vendor becomes an outage in your business.

 The swap itself rarely costs much. The expensive part is not knowing whether the new model is good enough, because "good" never got written down.

 Lock-in is mostly a testing problem. If you can't prove a cheaper model handles the job, you keep paying for the expensive one.

### How Do You Build a Model-Agnostic Layer?

 Model-agnostic is simple. Your workflow logic (triggers, data, guardrails, approvals) lives separately from the model doing the thinking, so the model becomes a setting instead of a foundation.

#### What that layer includes

- One place where the model is chosen, so a swap is a config change

- Prompts stored as versioned assets you own, outside any vendor tool

- A small test set per workflow: 20 to 50 real examples with known-good outputs

- Logging of inputs, outputs, cost, and failures so you can compare models on real traffic

- A fallback to a second provider when the first is down

### How Do You Match the Model to the Task?

 Frontier pricing is tiered for a reason. Plenty of steps in a workflow don't need the most capable model, and paying flagship rates for sorting email is waste.

- Volume work (classifying email, tagging tickets, extracting invoice fields): the cheapest, fastest tier

- Everyday drafting and routing: a balanced tier

- Hard reasoning (contract analysis, multi-step planning, edge cases): the flagship, only where it earns its cost

#### Illustrative Math
 A workflow that reads 5,000 emails a month at roughly 1,000 input tokens each is 5 million input tokens. At Luna's $0.20 per million, that's about $1 in input cost. At Terra's $2 per million, about $10. Output tokens add to both.

 The amounts are small at this scale, but the ratio holds as volume grows, which is why tier selection is worth getting right early. Prices as announced July 30, 2026; check current rates before budgeting.

### Where Should You Start?

 Audit each workflow for two things: which model it's hard-wired to, and whether anyone has tested an alternative. Pick your highest-volume workflow, write the test set, and run it against a cheaper tier. If it passes, you just cut that workflow's cost without touching the outcome.

 Do that once and the next price drop or model release is just a test run.

### Sources

- OpenAI, Advancing the price-performance frontier with GPT-5.6 (July 30, 2026)

#### Is your automation locked to one model?
 We'll audit your workflows, build the test sets, and set up routing so you capture price drops and new models as they ship.

 Source for pricing: OpenAI, July 30, 2026, as reported in industry news roundups.

# 2026's Biggest AI Trend for Professional Firms: Agents That Use Your Tools
By Derek Moore

Short answerAI agents can now operate your existing software the way an employee does, by clicking, typing, and navigating your CRM, accounting system, and scheduling tool, with no integration code. That matters most for firms whose tools have no API or only a thin one, because setup time no longer depends on company size.

 Think niche software. Practice-management tools, property platforms, and accounting systems are what real estate, finance, legal, and professional services firms depend on, and they rarely have clean APIs. Agents that operate the screens close that gap.

 For most of the last two years, "AI adoption" meant picking a chatbot or paying a developer to wire up an API between two systems that don't talk. Chatbots answer questions but don't do the work. API integrations eat engineering hours most firms can't justify for a single workflow.

 In 2026 there's a third option: agents that operate your existing software directly. They click, type, and navigate your CRM, accounting system, scheduling tool, and inbox the way a person does, with no integration code.

 That capability just crossed from "impressive demo" to "reliable enough to run unattended on real business processes." It's the biggest reason AI automation is finally landing at companies too small for an engineering team.

 No API

 needed to automate many workflows in software that lacks one

 Any Tool

 if a human can log in and click through it, an agent now can too

 ~66%

 agent task success on real computer tasks, up from 12% (Stanford AI Index 2026)

### Why Did "Just Integrate It" Never Work for Firms?

 The standard advice was to connect systems through their APIs: pull data from the CRM, push it into accounting, trigger a notification in project management. That works if you have a developer on staff, an integrator's budget, and software with a usable API.

 Most firms' stacks miss that bar. A lot of the tools running a $5-30M business (a niche scheduling app, an industry ERP, a legacy accounting package) have no API, a thin one, or one that takes a developer weeks to tame. That wall kept AI automation a large-enterprise perk.

### How Do Agents Operate Software Like a Person Does?

 AI models got reliable at computer use: reading a screen, deciding what to click, filling in a form, dealing with the surprise popup. An agent needs the same login you'd hand a new employee, and that's it.

 So the question for any task becomes: could someone log in and click through a known set of steps? If yes, an agent can take it, whether or not the software was ever "integration-friendly."

#### What this opens up for a typical firm

- Pulling new web-form leads into whatever CRM you use, however obscure

- Cross-checking an invoice against records in an accounting tool with no public API

- Updating records across two or three disconnected systems

- Running repetitive multi-step work (data entry, status checks, follow-ups) inside tools your team already knows

 The practical test: if you've ever said "I'd automate that, but our software doesn't have an API," this trend covers exactly that case. The constraint that used to end the conversation is gone.

### Why Does This Matter More for Firms Than Enterprises?

 Large enterprises could always afford custom integration work: dev teams, six-figure budgets, IT staff who maintain API connections full-time. Firms mostly couldn't, so AI automation felt built for someone else's budget.

 Agents that work through the existing interface level that out. A 15-person business and a 1,500-person business can automate a workflow in about the same setup time, because neither needs a bespoke integration first.

#### Don't Skip Governance
 An agent with login access to your CRM or accounting system needs the same guardrails as a new hire: scoped permissions, a clear list of what it can do without approval, and a defined point where it stops and asks a human. Lowering the integration barrier raises the stakes on oversight, and more businesses will hit that question sooner than they expect.

### How Do You Evaluate This for Your Business?

 List the workflows where your team logs into two or more systems and moves information between them by hand. Those used to need a custom integration and now don't. Rank them by frequency and time eaten, and start with the one that scores highest on both.

 Be skeptical of any vendor pitching this as fully hands-off from day one. A good rollout has a human reviewing the agent's work closely for the first few weeks, then widening its autonomy as it proves out (the same ramp you'd use for a new hire on a process that matters).

- Stanford HAI, The 2026 AI Index Report

 We'll map your current tools and show you where an agent could take over without a single custom integration.

URL: https://aismartr.com/blog-agentic-ai-multi-agent-systems-2026.html
# Agentic AI in 2026: Why Multi-Agent Systems Are Replacing the Single Chatbot
By Derek Moore

Short answerAI is moving from a single assistant to a team of agents with defined roles, and that team needs governance: scoped permissions, an audit trail, and a clear line where each agent stops. Firms that map a real workflow, split it into agent-sized pieces, and build the guardrails first get the most from it.

 What a team of agents looks like. At a real estate firm, one agent answers leads, one schedules showings, and one handles paperwork. On a finance team, one reads invoices, one matches POs, and one routes approvals. Each has a role, a limit, and a log.

 For the past few years, "adding AI" meant bolting a chatbot or copilot onto the business: one assistant that drafted emails, answered questions, or summarized documents when asked. That era is ending. Analysts and enterprise buyers now ask "how do we orchestrate a team of agents that each own a piece of the workflow?" instead of "which copilot should we use?"

 The shift changes what "AI automation" means, and what you should ask a vendor (or yourself) before spending another dollar on tools.

 1 → Many

 single copilots giving way to coordinated agent teams

 Assistant

 → "digital colleague" owning full workflow stages

 Governance

 now a deployment requirement

### What Changes When AI Moves From Copilot to Digital Colleague?

 The first wave of business AI was assistive: a chatbot that answered when you typed, a writing tool that suggested a sentence. A human drove every step.

 The current wave hands an agent a whole stage of a workflow and lets it run with oversight. The agent monitors the inbox, drafts the follow-up, schedules the send, and flags anything needing a human decision. That's a colleague you manage instead of a tool you operate.

 The practical test: if your AI still needs someone to open a tool and type a request every time, you're in the copilot era. If it watches for triggers and acts on its own within rules you've set, you're agentic.

### Why Isn't One Agent Enough Anymore?

 Real workflows rarely fit one skill set. A new website lead needs to be qualified, routed, scheduled, and followed up on: four jobs that suit purpose-built agents handing off to each other better than one generalist doing everything passably.

 That's the multi-agent shift. Small specialized agents each do one job well and pass work down the chain, the same reason a business hires a team instead of one person who does everything.

#### What a multi-agent setup typically looks like

- An intake agent that qualifies and routes incoming leads or requests

- A research agent that gathers the context the next step needs

- An execution agent that drafts, books, or updates records

- A review layer that catches anything outside its rules and brings in a human

### What Is Governance-as-Code, and Why Is It Now Required?

 More autonomy raises an obvious question: who's watching the agents? Enterprises are converging on governance-as-code: permissions, audit trails, and guardrails defined in the system itself instead of in policy documents people skim once.

 Each agent gets scoped, least-privilege access to only the systems it needs. Every action gets logged.

 There's a defined point where it must stop and ask a human. That separates a production-ready agentic system from a demo that breaks the first time it touches real customer data.

#### Why This Matters for Smaller Businesses Too
 Governance sounds like an enterprise problem, but it scales down. A 10-person business that hands an agent access to its CRM and inbox needs the same basic guardrails as a Fortune 500: scoped permissions, an audit trail, and a clear line where the agent stops and asks. The stakes are smaller and the principle is identical.

### What Does This Mean for Your Business?

 You don't need a five-agent orchestration system to benefit. The ceiling on what AI automation can do for you just moved. Workflows that needed a human babysitting every step between two or three tools can go to a coordinated set of agents, with a human checking in only at the decisions that matter.

 The businesses getting the most out of AI in 2026 mapped a real workflow, split it into agent-sized pieces, and built the guardrails before handing over the keys.

### Where Should You Start?

 Pick one workflow that bounces through three or more manual steps: lead intake, client onboarding, invoice processing. Map who or what should own each step. That map is the blueprint for your first multi-agent system, and a better starting point than "which AI tool should we buy?"

 Before an agent touches client data, read our guide to AI agent security risks and best practices.

 We'll map your highest-friction workflow and show you where agent handoffs would save the most time.

# Build vs. Buy: When Off-the-Shelf AI Tools Stop Being Enough
By Derek Moore

Short answerBuy when your need is common, your workflow is standard, and a tool already does about 90% of it. Build custom when the last 20%, the part that fits your firm's workflows, rules, and client data, is where the value sits. Generic tools get you most of the way fast, then run out of road.

 Where custom earns its keep. Real estate, finance, legal, and professional services firms run on specific forms, systems, and compliance rules. Generic tools weren't built around any of them.

 Every automation conversation hits the same fork: subscribe to a tool that already does this, or build something custom? Most businesses default to buying, and most of the time that's right. It's fast, cheap, and someone else maintains it.

 Eventually off-the-shelf tools stop fitting and start fighting you. You're bending your process around the software. Knowing where that line sits saves you from overpaying for a custom build you didn't need, and from burning six months stitching together subscriptions that were never going to do the job.

### When Is Buying the Right Call?

 If your need is common, your workflow is standard, and a tool already does 90% of it, buy. You shouldn't custom-build an email marketing platform, a CRM, or a scheduler. Thousands of companies already paid for that R&D, and the result beats what most businesses could build.

 Off-the-shelf also wins when speed matters. You can be live on a SaaS tool the afternoon you sign up. A custom build takes weeks at minimum.

 Need it by Friday? Buy.

#### Buy when

- Your workflow matches how 80% of businesses in your category operate

- The tool's roadmap is heading where you need to go anyway

- You need it live this week, not next quarter

- The subscription is trivial next to the time it saves

### Where Does Buying Break Down?

 The cracks show up between tools, not inside them. Your CRM doesn't talk to your scheduler the way you need.

 Your support tool can't trigger the exact sequence your business requires when a ticket arrives. You end up exporting CSVs, copy-pasting between tabs, and paying someone to be the human glue between systems that were never built to work together.

 That's a build problem wearing a buy problem's clothes. The gap between the tools is where the real cost lives.

 Watch for repetition. If your team repeats the same multi-step workaround several times a week because "the tools don't talk to each other," that workaround is the product you need. No vendor sells it off the shelf because it's specific to you.

### What Is the Hidden Cost of Generic Tools?

 A second failure mode is quieter. The tool works fine alone but forces your business to operate like every other customer.

 Generic chatbots give generic answers because they're trained on generic data. Generic workflow builders assume a generic process.

 If your edge lives in how you do things (pricing logic, client onboarding, compliance rules), a one-size-fits-all tool sands it off. You end up "automated" with output a customer can tell came from a template.

### What Does a Custom Build Actually Buy You?

 Custom beats off-the-shelf when it's built around your constraints instead of someone else's average customer. A custom integration connects the exact systems you use in the exact sequence you run them, with no one bridging the gap by hand. A fine-tuned model speaks in your voice.

 A purpose-built tool does the one odd thing your business needs that no SaaS vendor will prioritize, because you're an edge case to them and the main case to you.

#### Build when

- You're paying for several tools and a person to connect them by hand

- The workaround has become permanent

- Your edge lives in a process generic tools flatten

- The data or workflow is sensitive enough that a tighter, owned system matters

#### A Practical Test
 Add up what you spend on SaaS subscriptions for one workflow, plus the hours someone spends each month bridging the gaps between them. If that rivals the cost of a one-time custom build that removes the bridging entirely, you're choosing between paying forever and paying once.

### Where Should You Start?

 Skip the abstract debate. Map where your team does manual, repetitive work to connect tools that don't talk. That list is your build candidate pool.

 Build for that list and keep buying everything standard and well served. That stops you paying SaaS prices for a workaround that was never going to scale.

#### Not sure which side of the line you're on?
 We'll look at your current stack and tell you honestly where a tool will do the job and where it won't.
